lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Launch and planning: making and preparing for an appointment

objective: Learners draft a written plan and script for scheduling a routine health appointment (what to say, what questions to ask, what information to have ready) without placing a real call, so they build the skill in a low-pressure, private way before ever needing it for real.
scenario: Using a fictional but realistic prompt (a routine check-up the learner's household could plausibly need), the learner writes the exact opening line they would use to schedule it, lists the information a scheduler typically asks for, and writes three questions to ask once the appointment is set.
safetyNotes: No real appointment is scheduled and no real call is placed for this lesson; the deliverable is a written plan and script only.
The learner does not need to disclose any real health information, condition, or provider name to complete this lesson.

tasks.directions: Before drafting, write down what makes scheduling calls or messages feel awkward or hard.

prompts.text: What is the part of scheduling something over phone or message that you'd find hardest, and why?

tasks.directions: Draft the opening line and the information a scheduler typically needs.

prompts.text: Write the exact opening sentence you would say or type to schedule the appointment, clearly stating what you need and roughly when.
My draft lists the kind of information a scheduler usually asks for (such as the reason for the visit and available days/times), without needing real personal health details.

tasks.directions: Write three questions you would ask once the appointment is confirmed.

prompts.text: Write three specific questions you'd want answered before the appointment (for example, how to prepare, what to bring, or roughly how long it takes).

tasks.directions: Reflect on how the plan changes your comfort level.

prompts.text: Having written this out, what part of a real version of this task would you now feel ready for, and what part would you still want help with?

remediation: If the opening line is too vague to actually schedule anything (for example, just 'I need an appointment'), reteach by modeling a complete opening line with all three needed parts named explicitly: what you need, roughly when, and one piece of contact information, then have the learner rewrite their line following that same three-part structure.
extension: Have the learner write a second version of the plan for a scenario where the first available time doesn't work for their schedule, including what they would say to ask for an alternative.
